Findings.Comment: The retry guard is inverted relative to the previous `if !retryable(err) { return err }` and to the documented contract. On a realistic input — the endpoint returns 503 — `post` reports a transient (non-permanent) error, `retryable` returns true, and `Deliver` returns that error on the very first attempt, so no retry or backoff ever happens. Conversely a permanent rejection (4xx) is retried five times with sleeps before being wrapped as "giving up". Transient failures now fail fast and permanent ones are pointlessly retried, the opposite of the stated behaviour in the doc comment above `Deliver`.
Findings.Headline: Retry guard inverted: transient errors return immediately

Expected.why: Transient failures such as a 503 are now returned on the first attempt without any retry, while permanently rejected deliveries are retried five times with backoff.

Findings.Comment: `FetchDiff` detaches both the request and the body read from the caller's `ctx` by passing `context.Background()`. A caller that sets a deadline (or cancels on client disconnect) now gets no effect: `http.NewRequestWithContext` and `getTextCapped` are unbounded, so on a slow or stalled Bitbucket server the call blocks until the transport gives up instead of returning at the caller's deadline, and the `ctx` parameter is silently unused. This directly contradicts the doc comment on line 10, which states the caller's context bounds the whole operation including the body read.
Findings.Headline: FetchDiff ignores caller context and becomes unbounded
Findings.Suggestion: req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, u, nil)
Evidence: // The caller's context bounds the whole operation, including the body read.

Expected.why: ctx is a parameter but never used; context.Background() is passed to both NewRequestWithContext and getTextCapped, so the caller's timeout and cancellation cannot stop the request or the body read. Bitbucket has no Client.Timeout by design, which makes the caller's ctx the only bound on a 10 MiB diff.

Findings.Comment: `Hold` is meant to extend a session's lifetime in millisecond granularity — `Store.Touch` takes `ttlMillis` and forwards it to `PExpire` — but it passes `int64(d.Seconds())`. A caller that holds a session for, say, 30 seconds during a long-running export gets `Touch(ctx, id, 30)`, which sets a 30 ms TTL; the session is gone before the export finishes and the user is logged out mid-operation. The same truncation also turns any `d` below one second into 0, which `Store.Touch` rejects as a non-positive TTL.
Findings.Headline: Hold passes seconds where the store now expects milliseconds

Expected.why: Touch now takes milliseconds, so a hold of two hours sets a lifetime of 7.2 seconds and the session expires while the export it was meant to cover is still running.

Findings.Comment: This diff adds a plaintext database password literal to `application.yaml`, committed to the repo for the reporting datasource. Anyone with repository or artifact access (including anyone who pulls the built jar) obtains live credentials for `reporting-db.internal`, and the value is a default-looking one that will survive rotation only via another commit. The primary datasource above correctly uses `${INVENTORY_DB_PASSWORD}`; the reporting block should follow the same runtime lookup pattern instead of embedding the credential in source.
Findings.Headline: Hardcoded reporting DB password committed in application.yaml

Expected.why: The reporting replica's password is committed in the application config, readable by everyone with repository access, while the existing datasource takes its password from the environment.

Findings.Comment: The new `password` field in `DataSourceConfig` holds a plaintext database credential literal committed to the repository, and `reportingDataSource()` passes it straight to `HikariConfig.setPassword`. Anyone with repo or artifact access can read it, and it lives forever in git history even after it is rotated. This also contradicts the class javadoc ("Credentials come from the environment, injected by the platform at deploy time") and the adjacent `inventoryDataSource`, which injects `INVENTORY_DB_PASSWORD` via `@Value`. Use injected configuration for the reporting pool the same way.
Findings.Headline: Hardcoded database credential committed in the new `password` field
Evidence: return pool("reporting", reportingUrl, reportingUser, password, 4, true);

Expected.why: The reporting replica's password is committed in source, readable by everyone with repository access, while the class's own pattern reads credentials from the environment.

Findings.Comment:
This identity check compares two `Long` objects with `!=`, which is reference equality, not value equality. Repository and request layers both return boxed `Long` instances, and the `Long` cache only covers -128..127. A transfer created for account 100000L and cancelled by a request for the same account 100000L yields two distinct `Long` objects, so the comparison is false and a legitimate owner is rejected with `TransferAccessDeniedException`. Cancellation is only ever authorized for the owner, so this breaks the documented "Only the source account may cancel" contract for any account id outside the small-integer cache.

Suggested fix on the same line:
Findings.Headline: Long account ids compared with != instead of equals

Expected.why: Boxed Longs are compared by reference, so for any account id above 127 the owner's own cancellation is rejected as access denied.

Findings.Comment: The `defer r.mu.Unlock()` was replaced by a single `r.mu.Unlock()` on the success path, so the early return when the slug is unknown now returns while still holding `r.mu`. Calling `Disable("typo-slug", "reason")` once leaves the mutex locked forever: the next call to `Disable` (or any other method that takes `r.mu`) blocks on `r.mu.Lock()` and never returns. This is a deterministic deadlock on any lookup miss, not a rare race.
Findings.Headline: Disable leaks the mutex on the unknown-slug early return

Expected.why: The Unlock now runs only on the success path, so returning the unknown-team error leaves r.mu locked and every subsequent caller blocks forever.

Findings.Comment: The `r.Ticket == nil` guard no longer returns early; it just comments and falls through to `r.Ticket.Key`, which dereferences a nil pointer. Any `Result` built without a ticket — the case this guard was written for — panics on the next line instead of returning `r.Body`.
Findings.Headline: Nil ticket falls through to a nil dereference in Summarize
Evidence: // Ticket is optional; fall through to the shared renderer.

Findings.Comment: The comment "fall through to the shared renderer" contradicts the code that follows: there is no shared renderer, only a direct concatenation of `r.Ticket.Key`. Taken with the missing early return, it documents behaviour the function does not have and hides the nil-dereference path.
Findings.Headline: Comment in Summarize contradicts the code it guards
Evidence: // Ticket is optional; fall through to the shared renderer.

Expected.why: The nil branch no longer returns, so r.Ticket.Key panics whenever Ticket is nil. A reviewer may anchor on the dead check (19) or on the dereference (22).

Findings.Comment: Clamping `last` to `len(lines) + 1` makes `lines[first:last]` read one element past the end of `lines`. For any hunk whose trailing context runs to EOF — e.g. `lines` of 10 entries, `first = 8`, `n = 5` — `last` becomes 11, so `lines[8:11]` either panics with a slice-bounds error when `cap(lines) == len(lines)` (the common case for slices from `make` or `strings.Split`), or silently returns an element from beyond the file's content when the capacity is larger. The same failure hits the exact-fit case (`last == len(lines)`, previously a no-op) and the hunk-ends-at-EOF case (`first == len(lines)`, previously `nil`). The doc comment above the function says the window must stop at the last line of the file, which requires an exclusive bound of `len(lines)`, not `len(lines) + 1`.
Findings.Headline: Off-by-one clamp slices one element past end of lines

Expected.why: The clamp sets last to len(lines)+1, so the final slice expression lines[first:last] runs one past the length. With no spare capacity that panics; with spare capacity it silently yields a phantom trailing line, which is the quieter half of the bug.

Findings.Comment: The latest push removes `defer resp.Body.Close()`, so the response body from `c.http.Do(req)` is never closed on any path: on a non-2xx status the function returns at the `whoami: status %d` error, and on success it returns after `json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&u)` without closing. `WhoAmI` returns only `*User`, never `resp`, so no caller can close the body either. Every call therefore leaks the underlying TCP connection and a file descriptor; a caller that resolves accounts repeatedly (e.g. per request or in a loop) will exhaust the connection pool and the process's FD limit.
Findings.Headline: WhoAmI no longer closes the HTTP response body

Expected.why: The response body is never closed on any path, so the underlying connection is leaked on every call, successful or not.

Findings.Comment: Dropping `q.mu.Lock()` / `q.mu.Unlock()` around `q.depth = len(q.pending)` in `worker` makes this write unsynchronized while `Submit` and `Depth` both read/write `q.depth` under the same mutex. On any real workload where a job finishes concurrently with a `Submit` or `Depth` call, the goroutines race on `q.depth` (and on `q.pending` being read here while `Submit` appends): `-race` reports a data race, and the write can be reordered or lost so `Depth` reports a stale backlog count. The lock is still taken on every other access to these fields, so the removal also breaks the invariant the rest of the type relies on.
Findings.Headline: Unsynchronized write to Queue.depth after removing the mutex in worker

Expected.why: The worker goroutine writes q.depth and reads q.pending without holding q.mu, while Submit writes and Depth reads the same fields under the mutex; that is a data race.
The rejected promise leaves the try block before it settles, so the catch never runs and a provider outage fails every request instead of serving the expired table.

Findings.Comment: The commit error is now discarded, so `AddClaim` returns `nil` even when the transaction fails to commit. If the database connection drops or the commit is rejected at commit time (deferred constraint, serialization failure), the caller is told the claim was recorded while no row exists — silent data loss on a realistic failure path. The previous code returned the wrapped commit error; that behavior should be preserved.
Findings.Headline: AddClaim discards commit error and reports success on failure

Expected.why: tx.Commit's error is discarded, so a failed commit is reported to the caller as success and the claim silently does not exist.

Findings.Comment: The two error branches are now inverted relative to the documented contract. `ErrNoClaim` is described as what callers match on when a project has no owner yet, and `Owner`'s doc says callers separate "nobody owns it" from a database fault with `errors.Is`. After this swap, a genuine no-claim result wraps the raw `errNoRows` (so `errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim)` is false and callers treat it as a fault), while an actual database failure wraps `ErrNoClaim` (so callers treat a DB outage as "nobody owns it" and may proceed to claim or reassign the project). The two `return` lines need to be swapped back.
Findings.Headline: Owner() wraps ErrNoClaim on DB faults and raw errNoRows when unclaimed

Expected.why: The branches wrap each other's error: errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim) is now false when the project is genuinely unclaimed and true when the query failed, so a database fault is treated as an unowned project.
